sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Micropiles have been used successfully in a wide variety of geotechnical applications worldwide. This chapter provides an overview of the primary applications of micropiles, organized into two broad categories: (1) structural support applications (CASE 1) and (2) in-situ reinforcement applications (CASE 2). For each application category, the chapter describes the design concept, discusses advantages and limitations, and presents representative case histories from US and international practice. The versatility of micropiles stems from their small size, ability to be installed in virtually any ground condition, minimal noise and vibration during installation, and ability to work in access-restricted and low-headroom environments.
key_points: Applications organized into structural support (CASE 1) and in-situ reinforcement (CASE 2)
Micropile versatility derives from small size and adaptable installation methods
Can be installed in virtually any ground condition
Minimal noise and vibration compared to driven piles
Suitable for access-restricted and low-headroom environments
Case histories from both US and international practice are presented

sections.title: Structural Support of New Foundations
sections.body: Micropiles are used for structural support of new foundations where conventional deep foundations are impractical or uneconomical. Specific situations favoring micropiles for new construction include: (1) sites with difficult ground conditions such as karstic limestone, boulders, or highly variable subsurface profiles; (2) sites requiring minimal construction vibration to protect adjacent structures or vibration-sensitive equipment; (3) sites with limited access or restricted headroom such as bridge widening within existing structures; and (4) sites where high-capacity foundations are needed with minimal ground disturbance. Micropiles can support a wide range of structures including bridges, buildings, retaining walls, sound walls, and transmission towers. Design loads for individual micropiles in new construction applications typically range from 300 to 3000 kN, depending on the micropile diameter, reinforcement, grouting type, and ground conditions.

sections.title: Underpinning of Existing Structures
sections.body: Underpinning is one of the most common applications of micropiles and was the original application for which micropile technology was developed. Micropile underpinning involves the installation of micropiles through or adjacent to existing foundations to provide additional support or to transfer loads to deeper, more competent strata. Common reasons for underpinning include: (1) settlement distress due to consolidation, poor original design, or adjacent construction activities; (2) increased loading requirements due to change in use or structural modifications; (3) deterioration or damage to existing foundations; and (4) protection against future settlement from tunneling, adjacent excavation, or dewatering. Micropile underpinning offers significant advantages over conventional underpinning methods such as pit underpinning or jack-and-bracket systems. The small size of drilling equipment allows work within existing structures, and installation causes minimal disturbance to ongoing operations. Connections between micropiles and existing foundations are typically made by drilling through the existing footing or pile cap and grouting the micropile into the drilled hole.
key_points: Original and most common micropile application since the 1950s
Micropiles installed through or adjacent to existing foundations for additional support

Advantages over conventional underpinning: small equipment, minimal disruption

sections.title: Seismic Retrofit Applications
sections.body: Micropiles have been used extensively for seismic retrofit of existing foundations that have insufficient capacity to resist design earthquake forces. Seismic retrofit applications include: (1) providing additional axial capacity to resist increased vertical loads from overturning moments; (2) providing additional lateral resistance through battered micropiles or groups of vertical micropiles; (3) providing additional uplift capacity to resist tensile forces from seismic overturning; and (4) reducing the risk of foundation failure in liquefiable soils. Micropiles are particularly well-suited for seismic retrofit because they can be installed through and around existing structural elements with minimal disruption. In the United States, micropiles have been used for seismic retrofit of highway bridges in California, the Pacific Northwest, and the Central US (New Madrid Seismic Zone). Experience from the FOREVER project and the Trinh et al. (2004) study on inclined micropile foundations demonstrated that battered micropile groups can achieve fully ductile response under combined axial and lateral seismic loading when adequate pile cap reinforcement is provided.

sections.title: Slope Stabilization and Earth Retention
sections.body: Micropiles can be used for in-situ reinforcement of soil slopes (CASE 2 applications) using two general approaches. In Approach 1, battered micropiles are installed through the unstable slope to a depth below the potential slip surface and are connected at the ground surface by a concrete cap beam. The individual micropiles provide restoring forces through axial, shear, and bending resistance. The spacing of the micropiles along the slope is determined based on the stabilizing force required per lineal meter to achieve a target factor of safety. In Approach 2, a large number of micropiles are installed close together to create a coherent reinforced soil mass that behaves like a gravity retaining wall. The required restraining force is developed by sliding resistance along the base of the micropile group. Approach 1 is more commonly used in US practice, while Approach 2 has been applied primarily in European projects. Earth retention applications use micropiles in combination with structural elements to form retaining systems. Micropiles can also be used as soil nails in certain applications, although the design methodology differs from conventional soil nailing.
key_points: Two approaches: Approach 1 (battered piles with cap beam) and Approach 2 (coherent mass)
Approach 1: micropiles provide restoring forces through axial, shear, and bending resistance
Approach 2: many closely spaced micropiles create a gravity retaining wall effect
Approach 1 is more common in US practice
